lessons.title: Defensive Havens in a Slowdown: FMCG, Pharma, Utilities, and IT

body.text: A defensive sector is not one that never falls. It is one whose earnings keep coming when the economy slows. Whether it actually protects you depends on how much of that safety you have already paid for.

children.text: Lessons 3.2 and 3.3 covered the sectors that lead in recovery and expansion. This lesson completes the clock with the sectors investors run to when growth slows: FMCG, pharma, and power utilities, plus IT services, which Indian investors often treat as defensive but which behaves very differently. You will learn what makes a sector defensive, how to measure it, and why the "safe" trade can still lose money.
What Makes a Sector Defensive?
Stable demand. People keep buying soap, medicines, and electricity in a downturn.
Pricing power. Strong brands and essential products can pass on cost increases.
Low debt and high returns on capital. Little financial risk when credit tightens.
Steady cash flows and dividends. Investors value predictability when earnings elsewhere are being cut.
Low sensitivity to the market. Share prices tend to move less than the overall index.

markDefs.definition: A measure of how much a stock or index tends to move relative to the market. A beta of 1 means it moves in line with the market on average; 0.6 means it has tended to move about 60% as much; above 1 means it has amplified market moves.

children.text: That last trait has a number attached to it:
beta

body.caption: Beta compares a sector's returns with the Nifty 50's returns over a historical period

body.title: Beta vs the Nifty 50 (reported for mid 2026)
What Beta Implies
body.prompt: Suppose the Nifty 50 falls 20% in a slowdown, and a defensive sector index has a beta of 0.6. If the historical relationship holds, roughly how much would the sector index fall, in percent?
body.explanation: 0.6 multiplied by 20% gives about 12%. The sector would still fall, just less than the market. Beta is backward-looking and only an average, so a sector-specific shock, such as a regulatory change or a US tariff, can make a "low beta" index fall far more than this.

body.text: Notice where IT sits: a beta of about 0.97, almost the same as the market. Over the same period, IT has not behaved like a defensive sector. That is a clue we will return to at the end of this lesson.

children.text: FMCG: Steady Demand, Expensive Safety

Hindustan Unilever, Nestle India, ITC, Dabur, and Britannia sell products people buy every week. In a slowdown, consumers may trade down to smaller packs or cheaper brands, but they rarely stop buying. That makes FMCG earnings steadier than almost any other sector.

markDefs.definition: Growth in the quantity of goods sold, as opposed to growth driven by price increases. Volume growth shows genuine demand; price-led growth can mask weakening consumption.

children.text: The key thing to track is whether growth is coming from volume or price.
Volume growth
reflects real demand. Price-led growth can hide a squeeze on consumers, especially when inflation is high.

body.label: The price of safety
body.value: Nifty FMCG P/E 33.76 vs Nifty 50 P/E 20.20
body.context: Figures as reported for mid 2026 (FMCG) and 4 September 2026 (Nifty 50). Even after cooling from its seven-year median of about 41.8, FMCG still trades at a large premium to the market.

body.title: Measure the Valuation Premium
body.prompt: Using the figures above, by what percentage does the Nifty FMCG P/E of 33.76 exceed the Nifty 50 P/E of 20.20? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: 33.76 divided by 20.20 is about 1.67, a premium of about 67.1%. Investors pay that premium for steady earnings. The risk is that if growth disappoints, or if safe government bond yields rise, the premium can shrink and the share price can fall even while earnings hold up.

children.text: Pharma: Two Businesses Under One Label

Indian pharma combines a domestic branded medicines business, which is steady and grows with healthcare spending, and an export business, largely generic medicines for the US and other regulated markets, which follows its own cycle of pricing pressure, drug approvals, and regulatory inspections.

children.text: The US tariff announced in September 2025 shows why pharma's defensiveness is conditional. Because generics, the bulk of India's US exports, were exempt, the overall hit was limited. But companies with meaningful US branded or patented sales were more exposed. A defensive sector can still carry company-specific and policy risks that have nothing to do with the Indian cycle.
Power Utilities: Regulated Returns

NTPC, Power Grid, and similar utilities earn a regulated return on the equity they invest in approved projects. Under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission's tariff regulations for 2024 to 2029, that return is set at around 15% to 15.5% for conventional generation and transmission assets. Revenue is largely protected from demand swings, and costs such as fuel are generally passed through. That makes utilities steady in a slowdown, while India's rising power demand, a record 270.8 GW peak in May 2026, adds long-term growth.

body.text: Utilities behave partly like bonds. Their steady, regulated cash flows are valued against government bond yields, so when yields rise sharply, utility share prices can come under pressure even though their earnings are stable. Heavy capex plans also mean rising debt, which matters more when interest rates are high.

children.text: IT Services: Defensive or Not?

For years, Indian investors treated TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, and Wipro as defensives: debt-free, cash-rich, dividend-paying, and earning in dollars. In an Indian slowdown with a falling rupee, they often did hold up. But IT does not follow the Indian cycle. It follows technology spending in the US and Europe, and that makes it a global cyclical with a currency cushion.

body.caption: A weaker rupee raises rupee revenue and margins even if dollar revenue is flat

body.title: The Rupee Cushion
body.prompt: An IT company earns US$100 million a quarter. If the rupee weakens from ₹90.00 to ₹95.72 per dollar and dollar revenue is unchanged, by what percentage does rupee revenue rise? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Rupee revenue rises from ₹900 crore to about ₹957.2 crore, an increase of about 6.36%. That currency cushion is why IT often looks resilient when the rupee falls during Indian stress. But it cannot replace real demand growth, and costs such as onsite salaries and visa fees are also paid in dollars.

body.text: IT's defensive reputation has been tested by slow global tech spending, pressure from AI on traditional outsourcing work, and US visa policy. Low growth guidance, a beta close to the market, and a P/E below the Nifty 50 all say the market no longer treats IT as a safe haven. The rupee still helps, but defensiveness has to be earned by steady earnings, not assumed from history.

body.title: Go deeper: when defensive sectors fail to defend

children.text: Valuation. If defensives are already expensive going into a slowdown, their premium can compress, producing losses despite steady earnings.
Rising bond yields. Stable, bond-like businesses such as utilities and staples can fall when yields rise, because safe bonds become relatively more attractive.
Sector-specific shocks. A USFDA import alert, a US tariff, or a GST change can hit a "defensive" sector regardless of the cycle.

Input cost inflation. A stagflationary slowdown, with growth weak but inflation high, squeezes FMCG margins, which is why the Investment Clock favours defensive value over defensive growth in stagflation.
The wrong kind of slowdown. A global slowdown hurts IT and pharma exports; a domestic consumption slowdown hurts FMCG volumes. Match the defensive to the source of the slowdown.
Practice

body.title: Name the Measure
body.textWithBlank: An index that has historically moved about 60% as much as the Nifty 50 is said to have a ___ of 0.6.
body.explanation: Beta measures sensitivity to the market. Defensive sectors such as FMCG and pharma have had betas around 0.6, while IT was reported near 1.0 in mid 2026.

body.title: Choose the Right Haven
body.question: A slowdown is being caused mainly by weak US and European demand, while Indian domestic consumption is holding up and the rupee is stable. Which defensive sector is most exposed?
options: FMCG, because it sells everyday goods
Power utilities, because they earn regulated returns
IT services, because their revenue depends on global technology spending
Domestic branded pharma, because it depends on Indian healthcare spending
body.explanation: IT services earn most of their revenue from clients in the US and Europe, so a global slowdown hits their demand directly, and a stable rupee removes the usual currency cushion. FMCG, utilities, and domestic pharma depend mainly on Indian demand, which in this scenario is holding up.

cards.definition: A sector whose earnings remain relatively stable when economic growth slows, typically because demand for its products is essential.
Sensitivity to market moves. Below 1 means historically less volatile than the market; above 1, more volatile.
Growth in quantities sold. The best indicator of real consumer demand for FMCG.
The return a regulator allows a utility to earn on its invested equity, around 15% to 15.5% for many conventional assets under CERC rules for 2024 to 2029.
Revenue growth excluding the effect of exchange rate changes, used by IT companies to show underlying demand.
How much more expensive a sector is than the market, for example on P/E. High premiums reduce the protection defensives offer.

body.title: Building a Defensive Tilt
body.scenario: Your scorecard has moved from expansion to slowdown. Manufacturing and services PMI are falling, credit growth is decelerating, and CPI inflation is 5.8% because of high crude oil prices. The 10-year bond yield has risen 50 bps in six months. Nifty FMCG trades at a P/E about 65% above the Nifty 50, Nifty Pharma is near its long-term average, and IT is cheap but guiding to low growth. The rupee has weakened 5% in a year.
body.prompt: How would you think about FMCG, pharma, utilities, and IT as possible defensive tilts in this slowdown?
body.modelAnswer: This slowdown has stagflationary features, with weak growth, high inflation, and rising yields, so not every defensive fits. FMCG offers stable demand, but high crude-driven input costs can squeeze margins, and its large valuation premium could compress if yields keep rising, so its protection is weaker than usual. Pharma looks better placed: valuations near average, non-cyclical domestic demand, and a weaker rupee supporting export earnings, though company-specific US regulatory and tariff risks need checking. Utilities have regulated, largely pass-through earnings, but rising bond yields are a headwind for their valuations and their debt costs. IT benefits from the weaker rupee and cheap valuations, but low growth guidance and global demand risks mean it is not a pure haven; it only fits if the slowdown is domestic rather than global. A sensible approach is to prefer defensives with reasonable valuations and pricing power, check each against the specific source of the slowdown, and size positions rather than rotating everything at once. This is analysis, not a recommendation.

body.text: This lesson is educational. Company names are examples only and not recommendations. Beta, P/E, exchange rate, and export figures are as reported at the time of writing, come partly from secondary sources, and will change.

points: Defensive sectors have stable demand, pricing power, low debt, steady cash flows, and below-market beta
Reported betas in mid 2026: Nifty Pharma about 0.58 and Nifty FMCG about 0.61, while Nifty IT was about 0.97, close to the market
FMCG growth should be judged on volumes; in October to December 2025, rural volumes grew 2.9% and urban 2.3%, and the sector trades at a P/E premium of about 67% to the Nifty 50
Pharma combines steady domestic formulations with US generics exports; exports crossed US$31 billion in FY26, and the 2025 US tariff exempted generics
Power utilities earn regulated returns of around 15% to 15.5% under CERC rules, but their valuations are sensitive to bond yields
IT services are a global cyclical with a rupee cushion, not a pure defensive: low growth guidance, US visa costs, and AI pressure have tested that reputation
Defensives fail when valuations are stretched, yields rise, sector-specific shocks hit, or the slowdown comes from the wrong source
